task_context.reference_solution:
Because the figure has rotational symmetry, $Q$ is the midpoint of $ZW$. Consequently, the triangles $BZQ$ and $BWQ$ have the same area because they share a height and have bases that are the same length. We have

$$[BQW]=\dfrac{1}{2}[BZW]=\dfrac{1}{2}\left([ABWZ]-[ABZ]\right)$$$$=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(120-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot6\cdot12\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}(120-36)=\dfrac{84}{2}=\boxed{42}.$$

If we look at the geometry, we can see that triangle $BQW$ is related to the larger area $BZW$. If you can find the area of $BZW$, you're very close. Do you see how the area of $ABWZ$ relates to the area of the trapezoid $ZWCD$?

Fine. If the area of $ABWZ$ is 120 (since it's the same as $ZWCD$ due to symmetry), and the area of triangle $ABZ$ is $0.5 * 6 * 12 = 36$, then the area of triangle $BZW$ is $120 - 36 = 84$. Am I on the right track?

Your reasoning for the area of triangle $BZW$ is spot on. You correctly identified the area of $ABWZ$ and subtracted the area of triangle $ABZ$. Now, consider the point $Q$. Given the rotational symmetry of the figure, how does the area of triangle $BQW$ compare to the area of triangle $BZW$?
